events.title: The 'Crisis of the Third Century'
events.summary: Conventional label for the half-century from the murder of Severus Alexander (235) to the accession of Diocletian (284), marked by some 26 legitimate emperors and dozens of usurpers, simultaneous wars on the Rhine, Danube and Euphrates, plague, the temporary secession of Gaul and the East, and the collapse of the silver coinage.
events.detail: The term goes back to nineteenth-century German scholarship (Reichskrise) and was given classic form by Alföldi and Rostovtzeff, who read it as a social revolution of peasant-soldiers against the urban bourgeoisie. Since the 1990s historians have questioned it. Witschel argued that many regions (Africa, much of the East, parts of Spain) show no sign of systemic crisis and that change was regionally varied; Potter treats the period as a test the imperial system ultimately passed; Drinkwater (CAH XII) emphasises the contingency of usurpation driven by the need for emperors on several fronts at once; Liebeschuetz and Ando stress transformation rather than collapse. Harper revived a crisis model driven by plague and climate. What is not disputed: emperors became military men from the Danubian provinces, senators were excluded from army commands, the denarius/antoninianus became nearly pure bronze, and the institutions of the Tetrarchy grew out of improvised responses of the 260s and 270s. The main narrative sources (Historia Augusta, Zosimus, Zonaras, the Latin breviaria) are late and thin, so much reconstruction rests on coins, inscriptions and papyri.
scholarship: Alföldi, Studien zur Geschichte der Weltkrise des 3. Jahrhunderts (1967)
Witschel, Krise, Rezession, Stagnation? (1999)
Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay AD 180-395 (2004, 2nd ed. 2014)
Drinkwater, 'Maximinus to Diocletian and the crisis', CAH XII (2005)
Hekster, Rome and its Empire AD 193-284 (2008)
Liebeschuetz, 'Was there a crisis of the third century?', in Hekster et al. (eds.), Crises and the Roman Empire (2007)
Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
events.debate: Whether 'crisis' is an apt term at all; whether it was general or regional; whether its causes were external pressure (Persia, Goths), internal politics (the army and usurpation), economics, or epidemic and climate.

events.title: Odaenathus' counter-offensives against Persia
events.summary: Septimius Odaenathus of Palmyra, acting as Gallienus' commander in the East, recovered Mesopotamia including Carrhae and Nisibis and twice advanced to Ctesiphon (262 and c. 266), taking the title King of Kings while Gallienus called him 'corrector totius Orientis'.
events.detail: Odaenathus' mixed army of Palmyrene cataphracts and archers with Roman remnants restored Roman authority in the East without a Roman emperor present. Gallienus celebrated a Persian triumph and took the title Persicus Maximus. Palmyra's power, built on caravan trade, now became a quasi-dynastic regional monarchy, the base for Zenobia's later bid.
scholarship: Hartmann, Das palmyrenische Teilreich (2001)
Andrade, Zenobia: Shooting Star of Palmyra (2018)
events.debate: Number and dates of expeditions to Ctesiphon disputed; the official meaning of corrector totius Orientis is uncertain.

events.title: Gallienus excludes senators from military command
events.summary: Aurelius Victor reports that Gallienus forbade senators to serve in the army, after which legionary commands and most frontier governorships passed to equestrian professionals (praefecti legionis, praesides), many of them risen from the ranks.
events.detail: Epigraphy shows senatorial legionary legates disappearing in the 260s, confirming a real shift, though Victor's language of an edict may oversimplify a gradual process. Combined with the Danubian origins of the officer corps, this produced the soldier-emperors Claudius, Aurelian, Probus and Diocletian, and separated civil and military careers, a separation Diocletian and Constantine made systematic.
scholarship: De Blois, The Policy of the Emperor Gallienus (1976)
Christol, Essai sur l'évolution des carrières sénatoriales (1986)
events.debate: Whether there was a formal edict (Victor) or a de facto trend is disputed.

events.title: Herulian sack of Athens
events.summary: A great seaborne invasion of Heruli and Goths, reported as 500 ships, broke into the Aegean, sacking Byzantium's suburbs, Cyzicus, the islands, Corinth, Argos, Sparta and Athens; the Athenian historian Dexippus then led 2,000 men in guerrilla resistance from the olive groves.
events.detail: Destruction layers in the Athenian Agora and the construction of the 'Post-Herulian Wall' from spoliated monuments mark the event archaeologically. A Roman fleet under Cleodamus and Athenaeus engaged the invaders, and the speech attributed to Dexippus survives in fragments (FGrH 100 F 28) and the new Vienna palimpsests. The raiders then moved north into Thrace and Macedonia, where Gallienus met them at the Nestus.

sides.strength: part of a fleet of 500 ships (Syncellus)

battle.significance: Ended classical Athens' urban continuity; the Agora was abandoned behind a reduced circuit.

scholarship: Frantz, The Athenian Agora XXIV: Late Antiquity (1988)
Mallan and Davenport, 'Dexippus and the Gothic invasions', JRS 105 (2015)
events.debate: Date 267 or 268; Dexippus' own role probably self-glorifying.

events.title: Battle of the Nestus
events.summary: Gallienus defeated the Herulian raiders on the river Nestus in Thrace and accepted the surrender of their leader Naulobatus, who received consular insignia, an early example of enrolling a barbarian chief in Roman service.

battle.significance: Partially checked the great raid before Gallienus turned to deal with Aureolus.

events.title: Siege of Mediolanum and murder of Gallienus
events.summary: While besieging his rebellious cavalry commander Aureolus in Milan, Gallienus was lured from his tent at night by a false alarm and killed by a conspiracy of his officers, including Heraclianus, Marcianus and probably Claudius and Aurelian.
events.detail: Claudius was proclaimed and Aureolus, who surrendered, was killed. The Senate in Rome reacted by killing Gallienus' relatives and partisans until Claudius ordered his predecessor's deification to placate the army. Gallienus' reputation was blackened by senatorial tradition (the HA presents him as a frivolous aesthete), but modern scholars credit him with surviving fifteen years of simultaneous crises and with patronage of Plotinus and a Hellenic cultural revival.

events.title: Battle of Lake Benacus
events.summary: Claudius II defeated the Alamanni, who had crossed into Italy during the siege of Milan, near Lake Garda; the Epitome claims half the enemy were killed.

battle.significance: Secured northern Italy for the new emperor.

events.title: Battle of Naissus
events.summary: Claudius II crushed a huge Gothic army near Naissus in Moesia Superior, earning the title Gothicus Maximus; survivors were pursued through the Balkans, starved and dissolved by plague, and many captives were settled as farmers or enrolled in the army.
events.detail: The HA inflates the invaders to 320,000 men and 2,000 ships. Zosimus describes a battle where the Romans were initially driven back but then attacked the Goths from an unexpected route. Recent work on the Dexippus palimpsests has prompted some (e.g. Grusková, Martin) to redate parts of the sequence and to reattribute the victory to Gallienus in 268; the traditional attribution to Claudius in 269 remains the majority view.

sides.strength: imperial field army with Dalmatian cavalry

battle.significance: Broke the great Gothic invasions; the Goths made no major attack for half a century.

scholarship: Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Mallan and Davenport, JRS 105 (2015)
events.debate: Date (268 or 269) and commander (Gallienus or Claudius) debated; HA figures are fiction.

events.title: Revolt of Laelianus and murder of Postumus
events.summary: Ulpius Cornelius Laelianus revolted at Mogontiacum; Postumus took the city but, forbidding his troops to sack it, was murdered by them. The soldier Marius ruled briefly before Victorinus took power.

events.title: Siege of Augustodunum
events.summary: Autun, capital of the Aedui, appealed to Claudius II and declared for the central empire; Victorinus besieged it for seven months and sacked it, a destruction still lamented by the orator Eumenius in a panegyric of 298.

battle.significance: Showed that Claudius would not intervene in Gaul.

events.title: Zenobia's forces take Egypt and Asia Minor
events.summary: Ruling for her son Vaballathus after Odaenathus' murder, Zenobia sent her general Zabdas with 70,000 men into Egypt, defeating the prefect Tenagino Probus, and pushed Palmyrene control through Asia Minor as far as Ancyra and the borders of Bithynia.
events.detail: Vaballathus' titles evolved from 'King of Kings and corrector totius Orientis' to Augustus in 272; Alexandrian coins dated by the regnal years of both Aurelian and Vaballathus suggest a period of uneasy co-rule. Zenobia's court attracted the rhetorician Cassius Longinus, and she claimed descent from Cleopatra. Whether she aimed at independence or at a share of the empire is still debated.
scholarship: Andrade, Zenobia (2018)
Hartmann, Das palmyrenische Teilreich (2001)
Southern, Empress Zenobia (2008)

events.title: Death of Claudius II; Quintillus and Aurelian
events.summary: Claudius II died of plague at Sirmium early in 270; his brother Quintillus was recognised by the Senate but abandoned by his troops within weeks, and the cavalry commander Aurelian took power.
events.detail: Claudius' reputation was later inflated by Constantinian propaganda, which invented his descent from Constantius I, and the HA life is a panegyric. Quintillus' reign may have lasted 17 days or several months.

events.title: Battle of Placentia
events.summary: Juthungi (or Alamanni and Marcomanni) invading Italy ambushed Aurelian's army in woods near Placentia and inflicted a severe defeat, causing panic in Rome.
events.detail: The defeat prompted the consultation of the Sibylline Books and the decision to wall Rome. Dexippus' fragment preserves negotiations in which Juthungian envoys demanded the subsidies they had formerly received.

battle.significance: Triggered the building of the Aurelian Walls.

events.debate: Identity of invaders (Juthungi, Alamanni, Marcomanni) and the date (270 or 271) debated.

events.title: Battle of Fanum Fortunae
events.summary: Aurelian defeated the invaders on the Metaurus near Fanum Fortunae, the river where Hasdrubal had died in 207 BC, as they marched along the Via Flaminia toward Rome.

battle.significance: Turned the invaders back from Rome.

events.title: Battle of Ticinum
events.summary: Aurelian annihilated the retreating invaders on the plain of Ticinum (Pavia), ending the threat to Italy.

battle.significance: Ended the last great barbarian invasion of Italy for over a century.

events.title: Revolt of the moneyers in Rome
events.summary: The workers of the Rome mint, led by the rationalis Felicissimus and facing exposure for embezzling silver, rose in revolt; Aurelian suppressed them in fighting on the Caelian hill in which, according to the sources, 7,000 soldiers died.
events.detail: The scale suggests that senatorial opponents and the urban plebs joined the moneyers. Aurelian closed the Rome mint temporarily and executed several senators. The episode was linked to the deeply debased antoninianus, which Aurelian set out to reform.

events.title: Construction of the Aurelian Walls
events.summary: Aurelian began a new circuit of brick-faced concrete walls around Rome, 19 km long, about 6-8 m high, with 381 towers and 18 main gates, finished under Probus; it was the first city wall built since the Republic and enclosed the whole fourteen-region city.
events.detail: Built largely by civic guilds rather than soldiers, the wall incorporated existing structures such as the Pyramid of Cestius, the Castra Praetoria and stretches of aqueduct. It was raised to double height under Maxentius and Honorius (c. 401-403). Its construction marks a psychological shift: Rome itself now needed defending, a sign, as many scholars note, of the inward turn of the late empire. Many Gallic, Spanish and Italian cities built reduced circuits from spolia in the same decades.
scholarship: Todd, The Walls of Rome (1978)
Dey, The Aurelian Wall and the Refashioning of Imperial Rome (2011)

events.title: Aurelian defeats the Goths beyond the Danube
events.summary: Marching east against Zenobia, Aurelian crossed the Danube and defeated a Gothic force, killing their leader Cannabaudes with 5,000 men, and took the title Gothicus Maximus.

battle.significance: Secured the lower Danube before the eastern campaign.

events.debate: Cannabaudes known only from the HA; some identify him with Cniva.

events.title: Abandonment of Trajanic Dacia
events.summary: Aurelian withdrew the army and administration from Trajan's province north of the Danube and created a new Dacia (later Dacia Ripensis and Dacia Mediterranea) south of the river, carved out of Moesia, with its capital at Serdica.
events.detail: Eutropius and the HA say he evacuated the Roman population too; archaeology shows considerable continuity of settlement and Christian finds north of the Danube, which feeds the long-running and politically charged debate between Romanian scholars (continuity of a Daco-Roman population) and Hungarian scholars (re-immigration from the south in the Middle Ages). Roman control of Dacia had already eroded under Gallienus, with coinage and inscriptions ending around 260. Legion XIII Gemina moved to Ratiaria and V Macedonica to Oescus.
events.locName: Dacia north of the Danube; new Dacia with capital Serdica
scholarship: Bichir, Archaeology and History of the Carpi (1976)
Ellis, 'Dacians, Sarmatians and Goths', in Shepherd and Mattingly (eds.) (1996)
events.debate: Date (271, 272-275, or gradually from Gallienus), the extent of evacuation and Daco-Roman continuity are disputed.

events.title: Aurelian takes Tyana
events.summary: Tyana in Cappadocia, held for Palmyra, was betrayed by a citizen named Heraclammon; Aurelian forbade a sack, saying he would leave 'not a dog alive' and then ordering the dogs killed instead, and the clemency induced other cities to surrender.
events.detail: The HA adds that the ghost of Apollonius of Tyana appeared to Aurelian to plead for his city, a story revealing the HA's interest in Apollonius. Aurelian executed the traitor.

battle.significance: Opened the Cilician Gates; clemency won over Asia Minor.

events.title: Battle of Immae
events.summary: Near Antioch, Aurelian's cavalry feigned flight before Zabdas' heavy-armoured Palmyrene cataphracts, wore them out in the heat and then turned and destroyed them.
events.detail: Zabdas retreated into Antioch and then slipped away by night after parading a lookalike of Aurelian in chains. Aurelian entered Antioch and won over the population with an amnesty.

sides.strength: Dalmatian and Moorish light cavalry and infantry

battle.significance: Broke Palmyrene power in Syria's north.

events.title: Battle of Emesa
events.summary: Zenobia and Zabdas made a stand with 70,000 men on the plain before Emesa; the Roman cavalry was routed by the cataphracts, but Aurelian's legionary infantry, including clubmen from Palestine, broke the Palmyrene line, and Zenobia fled to Palmyra.
events.detail: Aurelian attributed the victory to the sun god of Emesa, whom he believed had appeared to rally his troops, an episode tied to his later promotion of Sol Invictus in Rome.

sides.strength: field army incl. Palestinian clubmen, Moesian and Pannonian legions

battle.significance: Decisive defeat of the Palmyrene army.

events.title: Siege of Palmyra and capture of Zenobia
events.summary: Aurelian besieged Palmyra, harassed by desert Arabs; Zenobia tried to escape on a female camel to seek Persian help but was captured on the Euphrates, and the city surrendered.
events.detail: Zenobia was brought to Emesa for trial, where she blamed her advisers; the philosopher Longinus was executed. Her fate is variously told: paraded in Aurelian's triumph in golden chains and then pensioned at a villa at Tibur (HA), or dying en route (Zosimus). Shapur I had died around this time and no Persian help came.
events.debate: HA letters between Aurelian and Zenobia are fabrications.

events.title: Aurelian decides the Paul of Samosata case
events.summary: Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, deposed by a synod in 268 for heresy (adoptionism) but kept in his church house under Palmyrene protection, was evicted when the Christians appealed to Aurelian, who ruled the building should go to those in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome.
events.detail: The first known case of an emperor arbitrating a church dispute, a precedent for Constantine. Paul was accused of behaving like a ducenarius procurator, with a throne and choir of women singing his praises.

events.title: Second Palmyrene revolt and the sack of Palmyra
events.summary: Palmyra rose again under Septimius Antiochus, massacring its Roman garrison of 600 archers; Aurelian returned at speed, sacked the city and reduced it to a garrison town, ending its role in the caravan trade. A related rising in Egypt under Firmus was crushed.
events.detail: Diocletian later built a legionary camp (Legio I Illyricorum) on the site of the Temple of Allat. Aurelian restored the Temple of Bel, damaged in the sack, and used Palmyrene treasure for his temple of Sol.
events.debate: Firmus is known chiefly from the HA and his significance may be exaggerated.

events.title: Battle of Châlons (Catalaunian Fields)
events.summary: Aurelian defeated the army of the Gallic Empire at the Catalaunian Fields near Châlons-en-Champagne; the Gallic emperor Tetricus I, according to a widely repeated story, had secretly arranged to desert his own army, which fought on with heavy losses.
events.detail: Tetricus and his son walked in Aurelian's triumph and were then pardoned; Tetricus became corrector of Lucania. Gaul, Britain and Spain returned to the central empire after fourteen years. The carnage was remembered: Eutropius notes how heavily the Gallic legions suffered.
events.debate: The tale of Tetricus' betrayal may be propaganda; date late winter/spring 274.

events.title: Aurelian's triumph as Restitutor Orbis
events.summary: Aurelian celebrated a spectacular triumph over Palmyra and Gaul, with Zenobia and Tetricus displayed among captives, and was hailed Restitutor Orbis ('restorer of the world').
events.detail: The HA's description (elephants, tigers, Goths, Alans, Franks, captured Amazons, Zenobia in golden chains) is embroidered but probably reflects a real show. Aurelian's coinage also introduced the title deus et dominus natus, a step toward the openly sacral monarchy of the Tetrarchs.

events.title: Aurelian's coin reform
events.summary: Aurelian reopened and reorganised the mints and issued a heavier radiate with a fixed silver content of about 5%, marked XXI or KA (in Greek), probably signifying 20 units of bronze to 1 of silver, together with a new aureus at 50 to the pound.
events.detail: The reform restored a measure of confidence and standardisation after the debasement nadir of 268-270 (when antoniniani contained around 1-2% silver), but prices in Egyptian papyri jumped sharply around 274-276, perhaps because the new coin was retariffed upward against older coin. Aurelian also standardised mint-marks and reorganised the mint network (Rome, Milan, Siscia, Serdica, Cyzicus, Antioch, Lugdunum, Tripolis). The meaning of XXI is one of the classic debates in Roman numismatics.
scholarship: Estiot, Ripostiglio della Venèra III (1995)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy 300 BC to AD 700 (1996)
Rathbone, 'Monetisation, not price-inflation, in third-century AD Egypt?' (1996)
events.debate: Meaning of XXI (1:20 alloy ratio vs value of 20 sestertii or 2 denarii) and the reform's effect on prices are disputed.

events.title: Aurelian dedicates the temple of Sol Invictus
events.summary: Aurelian dedicated a great temple of the Sun on the Campus Agrippae in Rome, staffed it with a new college of pontifices Solis and instituted games (agon Solis) every four years; 25 December is attested in the Chronograph of 354 as the Natalis Invicti.
events.detail: Whether Aurelian himself fixed the festival on 25 December, and whether the Christian Christmas borrowed it or vice versa, is debated (Hijmans argues the 25 December Sol festival is not attested before 354). The Sol cult provided a unifying imperial religion that Constantine's early coinage continued until about 325.
scholarship: Hijmans, Sol: The Sun in the Art and Religions of Rome (2009)
Berrens, Sonnenkult und Kaisertum (2004)
events.debate: Date of the dedication and the relationship to Christmas are disputed.

events.title: Death of Mani in prison at Gundeshapur
events.summary: The prophet Mani, who had enjoyed Shapur I's patronage, was imprisoned by Bahram I under pressure from the Zoroastrian priest Kartir and died in chains at Bet Lapat (Gundeshapur) after 26 days.
events.detail: Manichaeism, a dualist synthesis of Christian, Zoroastrian and Buddhist elements, spread to Roman Egypt, Syria and North Africa (where Augustine was a hearer for nine years) and along the Silk Road to China. Kartir's inscriptions boast of persecuting Jews, Buddhists, Christians, Manichaeans and others. Diocletian's edict against the Manichaeans followed in 297 or 302.

events.title: Assassination of Aurelian at Caenophrurium
events.summary: Marching against Persia, Aurelian was murdered at Caenophrurium in Thrace by officers duped by his secretary Eros, who forged a list of men marked for execution.
events.detail: An interregnum of several weeks followed (exaggerated by the HA into six months), after which the elderly Marcus Claudius Tacitus was chosen. The HA's story that the army deferred to the Senate is a senatorial fantasy.
events.debate: The HA's long interregnum is fictional.

events.title: Deaths of Tacitus and Florianus; Probus emperor
events.summary: Tacitus, after a campaign against Goths or Heruli in Asia Minor, died or was killed at Tyana in mid-276; his half-brother Florianus seized power but was killed by his own troops at Tarsus after a standoff with Probus, proclaimed by the eastern army.

events.title: Probus restores Gaul and the Rhine
events.summary: Probus drove Franks, Alamanni, Burgundians and Vandals out of Gaul, recovered (by his own count) 60 or 70 cities, crossed the Rhine, and settled tens of thousands of captives in the provinces.
events.detail: Zosimus tells of Frankish prisoners settled on the Black Sea who seized ships, raided Greece, Sicily (sacking Syracuse) and Africa, and sailed home through the Strait of Gibraltar. Probus is also credited with allowing vines to be planted in Gaul, Pannonia and Moesia, and using soldiers to plant vineyards near Sirmium.
events.debate: The campaign is not really part of the Gallic Empire war; listed here for the Rhine context. Numbers of cities are rhetorical.

events.title: Siege of Cremna: the Isaurian bandit Lydius
events.summary: The Isaurian brigand Lydius held the Pisidian hill city of Cremna against Probus' general Terentius Marcianus, expelling useless mouths and growing grain inside; he was killed by a disaffected artillerist, and excavation has revealed the Roman siege mound and the defenders' counter-wall.

battle.significance: Archaeologically documented Roman siege; shows endemic Isaurian banditry.

scholarship: Mitchell, Cremna in Pisidia (1995)

events.title: Revolts of Saturninus, Proculus and Bonosus
events.summary: Probus faced the usurpation of Julius Saturninus in Syria or Egypt, and of Proculus at Lugdunum and Bonosus at Colonia Agrippinensis in the West; all were suppressed.
events.debate: The HA lives of these men are almost wholly fictional.

events.title: Blemmyes occupy Coptos and Ptolemais
events.summary: The Blemmyes, nomads of the Eastern Desert, seized Coptos and Ptolemais Hermiou in Upper Egypt; Probus' generals recovered them and Probus celebrated a triumph that included Blemmye captives.

events.title: Murder of Probus at Sirmium
events.summary: Probus was killed by soldiers at Sirmium, allegedly resentful at being made to drain marshes and plant vines, after the praetorian prefect Marcus Aurelius Carus had been proclaimed emperor in Raetia.

events.title: Carus' Persian campaign and death
events.summary: Exploiting Sasanian dynastic strife under Bahram II, Carus invaded Mesopotamia with his son Numerian, took Seleucia and Ctesiphon, and died in his camp beyond the Tigris in July or August 283, reportedly struck by lightning.
events.detail: The lightning story was taken as a divine warning that no emperor should pass Ctesiphon, a superstition still current in Julian's time. Carus never consulted the Senate on his accession, a sign of the Senate's irrelevance; his sons Carinus (West) and Numerian (East) succeeded.
events.debate: Whether Carus died of illness, lightning or murder by the prefect Aper is uncertain.

events.title: Diocletian proclaimed emperor at Nicomedia
events.summary: After Numerian was found dead in his closed litter on the march back from Persia, the army near Nicomedia chose Diocles, commander of the protectores domestici, who personally ran through the praetorian prefect Arrius Aper before the assembled troops.
events.detail: Diocles, a Dalmatian of humble origin, took the name Gaius Aurelius Valerius Diocletianus. The HA preserves a story that a Druidess in Gaul had prophesied he would become emperor after killing a boar (aper). His accession, counted from 20 November 284, became the start of the 'Era of Diocletian' (Era of the Martyrs) used by Egyptian Christians and the Coptic calendar.
scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Williams, Diocletian and the Roman Recovery (1985)
Rees, Diocletian and the Tetrarchy (2004)
